segments.text: Part A. You hear a specialist physician talking to a patient called Julie Dooley. For questions 1 to 12, complete the notes with a word or short phrase. You now have 30 seconds to look at the notes.
Your GP says you've been to see him about a lump in your breast.
So, when did you first notice this lump?
Ten days ago.
I was doing my routine check when I was just so shocked to find it.
It's in my left breast.
I'm really worried because my mum died six months ago from breast cancer and I've been scared of getting it ever since
How old was your mum?
Do you know if anyone else in your family has had it?
I don't believe anyone else has. I don't remember
Mum?
Do you know if anyone else in your family has had it?
I don't believe anyone else has. I don't remember either of my parents talking about it affecting their own mums
Are you married?
Yes, but we separated nine months ago.
He went off with another woman and I'm on my own looking after my two children.
I've got a girl who's 14 and a 12 year old boy as well.
Have you ever been sick with anything serious before?
No, my health's always been very good.
I take it you're not on any medication then?
That's right, nothing.
But there is something else that's been playing on my mind since I noticed the lump.
I started remembering this pain I've been getting just here, in my chest.
In my chest. I never really thought anything of it before because it was kind of, oh I don't know, just very dull.
Like I'd pulled something. A muscle of some sort.
So I really wasn't very worried about it. I just thought it would go away in time.
But now, I don't know, do you think it could be a sign of something?
That's difficult for me to say until I examine you and we run some tests. Is there anything else you can tell me?
About the pain? Well, it seems to go to my back. I usually only notice it when I'm sitting in a chair.
Not a chair at the kitchen table, more like when I'm sitting in the lounge.
You know, something with a high back on it.
It did wake me from sleep once. It only lasted for about 15 to 20 minutes, but it was probably the worst I'd felt it.
There hasn't been anything else really. Like I said before, I'm usually pretty healthy.
You haven't had any nausea or vomiting with it? No shortness of breath?
Nothing else, except for what I mentioned. Oh, I do hope everything's all right.
Of course. Do you mind if I examine you now so I have an idea what we're dealing with?
No, that's fine.
Okay, there it is. Does that hurt?
No.
Right, it's quite solid, roughly two or three centimetres in length, I'd suggest.
We'll need to run some tests to confirm exactly what it is.
We can do those today, now actually,
and then wait a few days for the results to come in.
I'll need you to make a follow-up appointment on your way out today.
OK, that sounds fine.
I know I'm probably getting ahead of myself here,
but if it is cancer, I really don't want to lose the breast.
I'd hate to have to have a mastectomy.
I dread that probably more than anything else.
I really don't care what else happens, so long as I don't lose the breast.
My mother had chemotherapy after she was diagnosed with cancer and even though she lost all her hair, at least it grew back.
I'd still be willing to try it.
Okay, well, you are jumping in a bit early here, but there may be options.
First, let's run the test and wait for the results.
